claim: Malaria had an estimated 241 million cases in 2020.
source: Malaria remains one of the most life-threatening infectious diseases in the world, with estimated 241 million cases and 627,000 related deaths in 2020 (World health organization, 2021).
evidence: Cited from World Health Organization 2021 report

claim: Malaria had an estimated 627,000 related deaths in 2020.
source: Malaria remains one of the most life-threatening infectious diseases in the world, with estimated 241 million cases and 627,000 related deaths in 2020 (World health organization, 2021).
evidence: Cited from World Health Organization 2021 report

claim: Plasmodium falciparum is the most lethal human malaria species.
source: While the most lethal human malaria species, Plasmodium falciparum is able to infect both, mature erythrocytes and immature reticulocytes, the most widespread parasite Plasmodium vivax is restricted to invade the latter (Garnham, 1966; Kitchen, 1938; Chwatt, 1948).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garnham 1966, Kitchen 1938, and Chwatt 1948

claim: Plasmodium falciparum can infect both mature erythrocytes and immature reticulocytes.
source: While the most lethal human malaria species, Plasmodium falciparum is able to infect both, mature erythrocytes and immature reticulocytes, the most widespread parasite Plasmodium vivax is restricted to invade the latter (Garnham, 1966; Kitchen, 1938; Chwatt, 1948).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garnham 1966, Kitchen 1938, and Chwatt 1948

claim: Plasmodium vivax is restricted to invading reticulocytes.
source: While the most lethal human malaria species, Plasmodium falciparum is able to infect both, mature erythrocytes and immature reticulocytes, the most widespread parasite Plasmodium vivax is restricted to invade the latter (Garnham, 1966; Kitchen, 1938; Chwatt, 1948).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garnham 1966, Kitchen 1938, and Chwatt 1948

claim: Erythropoiesis primarily takes place in the bone marrow.
source: The formation of RBCs, known as erythropoiesis, primarily takes place in the bone marrow, where hematopoietic stem cells give rise to multipotent progenitors that stepwise differentiate into erythroblasts and reticulocytes (Moras et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Moras et al. 2017

claim: Early reticulocytes constitute 1-3% of circulating RBCs.
source: Early reticulocytes egress from the bone marrow and constitute 1–3% of circulating RBCs before they develop into mature erythrocytes (Chin-Yee et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from Chin-Yee et al. 1991

claim: Ter119 is induced in erythroblasts and persistently expressed during erythropoiesis.
source: While the erythroid lineage marker Ter119 is induced in erythroblasts and subsequently persistently expressed, expression of the transferrin receptor 1 (CD71) gets lost during the transition from reticulocytes to mature erythrocytes (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Chen et al. 2009

claim: CD71 expression is lost during the transition from reticulocytes to mature erythrocytes.
source: While the erythroid lineage marker Ter119 is induced in erythroblasts and subsequently persistently expressed, expression of the transferrin receptor 1 (CD71) gets lost during the transition from reticulocytes to mature erythrocytes (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Chen et al. 2009

claim: Hepcidin expression in the liver is upregulated upon Plasmodium blood stage infection.
source: Upon Plasmodium blood stage infection, hepcidin expression in the liver is upregulated, which in turn modulates parasitemia, disease outcome, and superinfection (Howard et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011; Portugal et al., 2011; Spottiswoode et al., 2014), fully supporting clinical studies that found associations of asymptomatic P. falciparum and P. vivax parasitemia with increased hepcidin concentrations and anemia (de Mast et al., 2010; Casals-Pascual et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from Howard et al. 2007, Wang et al. 2011, Portugal et al. 2011, and Spottiswoode et al. 2014

claim: Upregulated hepcidin modulates parasitemia, disease outcome, and superinfection during Plasmodium infection.
source: Upon Plasmodium blood stage infection, hepcidin expression in the liver is upregulated, which in turn modulates parasitemia, disease outcome, and superinfection (Howard et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011; Portugal et al., 2011; Spottiswoode et al., 2014), fully supporting clinical studies that found associations of asymptomatic P. falciparum and P. vivax parasitemia with increased hepcidin concentrations and anemia (de Mast et al., 2010; Casals-Pascual et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from Howard et al. 2007, Wang et al. 2011, Portugal et al. 2011, and Spottiswoode et al. 2014

claim: Asymptomatic P. falciparum and P. vivax parasitemia are associated with increased hepcidin concentrations and anemia.
source: Upon Plasmodium blood stage infection, hepcidin expression in the liver is upregulated, which in turn modulates parasitemia, disease outcome, and superinfection (Howard et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011; Portugal et al., 2011; Spottiswoode et al., 2014), fully supporting clinical studies that found associations of asymptomatic P. falciparum and P. vivax parasitemia with increased hepcidin concentrations and anemia (de Mast et al., 2010; Casals-Pascual et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from de Mast et al. 2010 and Casals-Pascual et al. 2012

claim: CD4+ T cells play a crucial role in regulating the immune response during the erythrocytic stage of malaria.
source: During the erythrocytic stage of malaria, CD4+ T cells play a crucial role in regulating the immune response.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript as established knowledge

claim: CD4+ T cells activate macrophages by secreting IFN-γ during malaria.
source: By secreting IFN-γ, they activate other immune cells, for example, macrophages, which are necessary for parasite clearance and control.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the manuscript

claim: CD4+ T cells provide help for B cells to induce protective responses against blood-stage parasites.
source: Moreover, CD4+ T cells provide help for B cells to induce protective responses against the blood-stage parasites (Perez-Mazliah and Langhorne, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Perez-Mazliah and Langhorne 2014

claim: Modulations of the sphingolipid metabolism enhance T cell activity during Plasmodium yoelii infection.
source: Recently, we showed that modulations of the sphingolipid (SL) metabolism enhance T cell activity during Plasmodium yoelii infection (Hose et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Hose et al. 2019, which is the authors' previous work

claim: Acid ceramidase is localized in the lysosomes.
source: Ac is localized in the lysosomes, where it preferentially hydrolyzes ceramides with medium-chain length (C12–C16) (Ferlinz et al., 2001; Momoi et al., 1982).
evidence: Cited from Ferlinz et al. 2001 and Momoi et al. 1982

claim: Acid ceramidase preferentially hydrolyzes ceramides with medium-chain length (C12-C16).
source: Ac is localized in the lysosomes, where it preferentially hydrolyzes ceramides with medium-chain length (C12–C16) (Ferlinz et al., 2001; Momoi et al., 1982).
evidence: Cited from Ferlinz et al. 2001 and Momoi et al. 1982

claim: Mutations in the ASAH1 gene can lead to Farber disease.
source: Mutations in the ASAH1 gene can lead to two different rare diseases, the lysosomal storage disorder Farber disease (FD) and an epileptic disorder called spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME) (Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Yu et al. 2018

claim: Mutations in the ASAH1 gene can lead to spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME).
source: Mutations in the ASAH1 gene can lead to two different rare diseases, the lysosomal storage disorder Farber disease (FD) and an epileptic disorder called spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME) (Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Yu et al. 2018

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Ac by ceranib-2 decreases measles virus replication in vitro.
source: While the pharmacological inhibition of Ac by ceranib-2 decreases measles virus replication in vitro (Grafen et al., 2019), genetic overexpression of Ac rescues cystic fibrosis mice from pulmonary Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in vivo (Becker et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Grafen et al. 2019

claim: Genetic overexpression of Ac rescues cystic fibrosis mice from pulmonary Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in vivo.
source: While the pharmacological inhibition of Ac by ceranib-2 decreases measles virus replication in vitro (Grafen et al., 2019), genetic overexpression of Ac rescues cystic fibrosis mice from pulmonary Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in vivo (Becker et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Becker et al. 2021

claim: Ac expression in macrophages limits the propagation of herpes simplex virus type 1.
source: Lang et al., 2020 recently showed that Ac expression in macrophages limits the propagation of herpes simplex virus type 1 and protects mice from severe course of infection.
evidence: Cited from Lang et al. 2020

claim: Ac expression in macrophages protects mice from severe course of herpes simplex virus type 1 infection.
source: Lang et al., 2020 recently showed that Ac expression in macrophages limits the propagation of herpes simplex virus type 1 and protects mice from severe course of infection.
evidence: Cited from Lang et al. 2020

claim: Ceramide concentrations were significantly increased in spleens from Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT mice.
source: Consequently, ceramide concentrations determined by mass spectrometry were significantly increased in spleens from Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Measured by mass spectrometry and shown in Figure 1C

claim: Ac KO mice showed significantly reduced parasitemia on days 3 and 7 post infection with P. yoelii.
source: Interestingly, Ac KO mice showed significantly reduced parasitemia on days 3 and 7 post infection (p.i.) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by parasitemia measurements shown in Figure 2A

claim: Differences in parasitemia between Ac KO and Ac WT mice were no longer detectable 10 and 14 days post infection.
source: However, these differences were no longer detectable 10 and 14 days p.i.
evidence: Stated based on parasitemia data in Figure 2A

claim: Spleen weights of Ac KO mice were tremendously decreased compared to Ac WT mice 7 days post infection.
source: Well in line with the observed effect on parasitemia, spleen weights of Ac KO mice were tremendously decreased compared to those of Ac WT mice 7 days p.i., but no longer differed on day 14 p.i. (Figure 2B).
evidence: Measured spleen weights shown in Figure 2B

claim: Spleen weights of Ac KO and Ac WT mice no longer differed on day 14 post infection.
source: Well in line with the observed effect on parasitemia, spleen weights of Ac KO mice were tremendously decreased compared to those of Ac WT mice 7 days p.i., but no longer differed on day 14 p.i. (Figure 2B).
evidence: Measured spleen weights shown in Figure 2B

claim: Frequencies of CD4+Foxp3-expressing regulatory T cells were significantly increased in spleen of Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT littermates 7 days post infection.
source: While frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells did not differ between P. yoelii-infected Ac WT and Ac KO mice, we found significantly increased frequencies of CD4+Foxp3-expressing regulatory T cells (Tregs) in spleen of Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT littermates (Figure 2C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from Ac KO mice showed decreased expression of Ki67, CD49d, CD11a, and PD1 at 7 days post infection.
source: Interestingly, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from Ac KO mice showed decreased expression of marker molecules associated with T cell activation, namely, Ki67, CD49d, CD11a, and PD1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D

claim: T cell-specific Ac ablation had no impact on the course of P. yoelii infection.
source: However, T cell-specific Ac ablation had no impact on the course of P. yoelii infection as Ac CD4cre KO (Asah1/Cd4cre/+) and Ac CD4cre WT (Asah1/Cd4+/+) mice showed similar spleen weights and parasitemia 7 and 14 days p.i. (Figure 3B).
evidence: Parasitemia and spleen weight data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Myeloid cell-specific Ac ablation did not significantly affect parasitemia and spleen weight during P. yoelii infection.
source: However, upon P. yoelii infection, Ac Lyz2cre KO (Asah1/Lyz2cre/+) mice and Ac Lyz2cre WT (Asah1/Lyz2+/+) littermates did not significantly differ regarding parasitemia and spleen weight (Figure 3D).
evidence: Parasitemia and spleen weight data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Reticulocytes were dramatically reduced in blood of noninfected Ac KO mice.
source: Strikingly, reticulocytes were dramatically reduced in blood of noninfected Ac KO mice (Figure 4A, d0).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Reticulocytes were almost absent on days 0 and 3 post infection in Ac KO mice.
source: While they were almost absent on days 0 and 3 p.i., frequencies rapidly increased in Ac KO mice 7 days p.i., resulting in equal percentages of reticulocytes in Ac WT and Ac KO mice 10 days p.i. (Figure 4B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Reticulocyte frequencies rapidly increased in Ac KO mice 7 days post infection.
source: While they were almost absent on days 0 and 3 p.i., frequencies rapidly increased in Ac KO mice 7 days p.i., resulting in equal percentages of reticulocytes in Ac WT and Ac KO mice 10 days p.i. (Figure 4B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Ac WT and Ac KO mice had equal percentages of reticulocytes 10 days post infection.
source: While they were almost absent on days 0 and 3 p.i., frequencies rapidly increased in Ac KO mice 7 days p.i., resulting in equal percentages of reticulocytes in Ac WT and Ac KO mice 10 days p.i. (Figure 4B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Erythroblasts and reticulocytes were hardly detectable in bone marrow of noninfected Ac KO mice on day 0.
source: As depicted in Figure 4D, erythroblasts and reticulocytes were hardly detectable in bone marrow of noninfected Ac KO mice on day 0 (left panel).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Percentages of erythroblasts and reticulocytes were increasing 7 days post infection in bone marrow of P. yoelii-infected Ac KO mice.
source: Consistent with raising reticulocyte frequencies in the blood (Figure 4B), percentages of erythroblasts and reticulocytes were increasing 7 days p.i. in bone marrow of P. yoelii-infected Ac KO mice, but they were still reduced when compared to infected Ac WT mice (Figure 4D, right panel).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Erythroblasts and reticulocytes were still reduced in Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT mice 7 days post infection.
source: Consistent with raising reticulocyte frequencies in the blood (Figure 4B), percentages of erythroblasts and reticulocytes were increasing 7 days p.i. in bone marrow of P. yoelii-infected Ac KO mice, but they were still reduced when compared to infected Ac WT mice (Figure 4D, right panel).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Ac expression was still absent in Ac KO mice 7 and 10 days post infection.
source: As validated by RT-qPCR, Ac expression was still absent in Ac KO mice 7 and 10 days p.i. (Figure 5A).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Neutral ceramidase (Nc) was upregulated after induction of the Ac KO.
source: We found the neutral ceramidase (Nc) to be upregulated after induction of the Ac KO (Figure 5B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Ceramide levels were significantly higher in bone marrow of Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT littermates 7 days post infection.
source: However, analysis of ceramide levels in bone marrow of Ac WT and Ac KO mice revealed significantly higher ceramide concentrations in bone marrow of Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT littermates 7 days p.i. (Figure 5C, right panel), similar to those measured on day 0 (Figure 5C, left panel).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Elevated Nc expression in Ac KO mice is not sufficient to completely compensate for Ac deficiency with regard to the ceramide content.
source: This suggests that elevated Nc expression in Ac KO mice is not sufficient to completely compensate for Ac deficiency with regard to the ceramide content.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ceramide levels remain elevated despite increased Nc expression

claim: Sphingomyelin levels were decreased in bone marrow of Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT mice on day 0.
source: While sphingomyelin levels were decreased in bone marrow of Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT mice on day 0 (Figure 5D, left panel), they were significantly enhanced on day 7 in the presence (Figure 5D, right panel) and absence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) of the infection, correlating with increasing reticulocyte frequencies observed before.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Sphingomyelin levels were significantly enhanced in bone marrow of Ac KO mice on day 7.
source: While sphingomyelin levels were decreased in bone marrow of Ac KO mice compared to Ac WT mice on day 0 (Figure 5D, left panel), they were significantly enhanced on day 7 in the presence (Figure 5D, right panel) and absence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) of the infection, correlating with increasing reticulocyte frequencies observed before.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Ac KO mice showed slightly increased sphingosine and significantly elevated S1P contents on day 0 compared to Ac WT littermates.
source: Moreover, Ac KO mice showed slightly increased sphingosine and significantly elevated S1P contents on day 0 in comparison to Ac WT littermates, while levels were similar 7 days p.i. (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 5E and 5F

claim: Sphingosine and S1P levels were similar in Ac KO and Ac WT mice 7 days post infection.
source: Moreover, Ac KO mice showed slightly increased sphingosine and significantly elevated S1P contents on day 0 in comparison to Ac WT littermates, while levels were similar 7 days p.i. (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 5E and 5F

claim: Carmofur is a potent inhibitor of Ac activity in mice.
source: Studies by Realini et al., 2013 showed that the antineoplastic drug carmofur is a potent inhibitor of Ac activity in mice.
evidence: Cited from Realini et al. 2013

claim: Carmofur-treated mice showed a strong reduction in parasitemia during P. yoelii infection.
source: Strikingly, carmofur-treated mice showed a strong reduction in parasitemia (Figure 6B).
evidence: Parasitemia data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Spleen weights of carmofur-treated mice were significantly reduced on day 7 post infection.
source: Moreover, spleen weights of carmofur-treated mice were significantly reduced on day 7 p.i. (Figure 6C).
evidence: Spleen weight data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Ceramide contents were significantly increased upon carmofur treatment in P. yoelii-infected mice 7 days post infection.
source: Indeed, ceramide contents were significantly increased upon carmofur treatment in P. yoelii-infected mice 7 days p.i. (Figure 6D) and noninfected mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) compared to control mice, whereas sphingosine, S1P, and sphingomyelin levels were similar in all groups.

claim: Carmofur-treated mice showed significantly reduced reticulocyte frequencies compared to vehicle-treated mice on days 3, 7, and 10 post infection.
source: While there is a tendency of decreased reticulocytes on day 0, carmofur-treated mice showed significantly reduced reticulocyte frequencies compared to vehicle-treated mice on days 3, 7, and 10 p.i. (Figure 6E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Carmofur treatment led to an altered erythropoiesis in bone marrow with lower relative numbers of erythroblasts and increased percentages of erythrocytes.
source: Furthermore, carmofur treatment led to an altered erythropoiesis in bone marrow with lower relative numbers of erythroblasts and increased percentages of erythrocytes compared to vehicle control 3, 7, and 10 days p.i. (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F and supplementary figures

claim: Plasmodium genomes do not encode candidate acid ceramidases.

claim: The effects of carmofur can be solely attributed to the inhibition of host cell Ac.
source: Hence, we conclude that the effects of carmofur can be solely attributed to the inhibition of host cell Ac.

claim: Mice showed significantly reduced reticulocyte frequencies after carmofur therapy 7, 10, and 14 days post infection.
source: As depicted in Figure 7B, mice showed significantly reduced reticulocyte frequencies after carmofur therapy 7, 10, and 14 days p.i.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Therapeutic carmofur treatment was accompanied by a strongly alleviated parasitemia.

claim: Spleen weights of carmofur-treated mice were decreased compared to vehicle control in the therapeutic treatment experiment.

claim: Carmofur-treated mice showed similar or even slightly higher RBC counts than vehicle-treated mice during infection.

claim: Carmofur-treated mice did not suffer from a more severe anemia.
source: Although carmofur therapy seems to reduce the production of reticulocytes, carmofur-treated mice showed similar or even slightly higher RBC counts than vehicle-treated mice during infection, indicating that they did not suffer from a more severe anemia (Figure 7E).

claim: P. yoelii parasites primarily infect reticulocytes, which are defined as Ter119+CD71+.
source: P. yoelii parasites primarily infect reticulocytes, which are defined as Ter119+CD71+ (Martín-Jaular et al., 2013).

claim: Long-chain ceramides (C22, C24:0, and C24:1) induce erythroid differentiation in bone marrow cells of rats.
source: While long-chain ceramides (C22, C24:0, and C24:1) are described to induce erythroid differentiation in bone marrow cells of rats (Clayton et al., 1974), the treatment with C2 ceramide or bacterial ceramide-generating sphingomyelinase resulted in the inhibition of erythropoiesis in human bone marrow cells (Dallalio et al., 1999).

claim: Treatment with C2 ceramide or bacterial ceramide-generating sphingomyelinase resulted in the inhibition of erythropoiesis in human bone marrow cells.
source: While long-chain ceramides (C22, C24:0, and C24:1) are described to induce erythroid differentiation in bone marrow cells of rats (Clayton et al., 1974), the treatment with C2 ceramide or bacterial ceramide-generating sphingomyelinase resulted in the inhibition of erythropoiesis in human bone marrow cells (Dallalio et al., 1999).

claim: C6 ceramide efficiently inhibits growth of P. falciparum parasites in a dose-dependent manner in vitro.
source: C6 ceramide has been shown to efficiently inhibit growth of P. falciparum parasites in a dose-dependent manner in vitro by reducing cytosolic glutathione levels and thereby inducing death of the parasites (Pankova-Kholmyansky et al., 2003).

claim: C6 ceramide inhibits P. falciparum growth by reducing cytosolic glutathione levels.
source: C6 ceramide has been shown to efficiently inhibit growth of P. falciparum parasites in a dose-dependent manner in vitro by reducing cytosolic glutathione levels and thereby inducing death of the parasites (Pankova-Kholmyansky et al., 2003).

claim: The cytotoxic effect of C6 ceramide on P. falciparum was abolished by addition of S1P.
source: This cytotoxic effect was abolished by addition of S1P, a downstream metabolite of ceramide and sphingosine, respectively.

claim: P. falciparum parasites strictly depend on the erythrocyte endogenous S1P pool for their intracellular development.

source: Carmofur has been developed and widely used in Japan to treat patients suffering from carcinomas of the gastrointestinal tract and breast.

claim: Ac-deficient mice show dysregulated erythropoiesis with reduced numbers of reticulocytes.

claim: Administration of the Ac inhibitor carmofur to wildtype mice has similar effects on P. yoelii infection and erythropoiesis as genetic Ac ablation.

evidence: Summary statement based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Therapeutic carmofur treatment after manifestation of P. yoelii infection is efficient in reducing parasitemia.

claim: Ac and ceramide are involved in controlling P. yoelii infection by regulating red blood cell development.

claim: The genetic ablation of Ac is embryonically lethal in mice.

claim: Reticulocytes are the preferred host cells of P. yoelii.

claim: Sphingomyelin increases the number of reticulocytes in mice.

claim: Elevated sphingomyelin concentrations might be responsible for resumption of erythropoiesis in Ac KO mice.

claim: The lower parasite load in the early phase of infection is due to highly reduced reticulocyte frequencies in blood of Ac KO mice.

claim: Carmofur treatment beneficially influences the balance between parasite burden and RBC production.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Ac might represent a novel therapeutic strategy to conquer malaria.

claim: Cell-intrinsic Ac activity plays an important role during erythropoiesis.

claim: Ceramide is a central hub in the sphingolipid network.

claim: Sphingosine can be phosphorylated by sphingosine kinases to form S1P.

claim: Five different human ceramidases have been described according to their pH optimum.
source: So far, five different human ceramidases have been described according to their pH optimum: acid ceramidase (Ac, N-acylsphingosine amidohydrolase 1, ASAH1), neutral ceramidase (Nc, ASAH2), and alkaline ceramidase 1–3 (Acer1-3, ACER1-3), each having a murine counterpart (Mao and Obeid, 2008).
evidence: Cited from Mao and Obeid 2008

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells give rise to multipotent progenitors that stepwise differentiate into erythroblasts and reticulocytes.
source: The formation of RBCs, known as erythropoiesis, primarily takes place in the bone marrow, where hematopoietic stem cells give rise to multipotent progenitors that stepwise differentiate into erythroblasts and reticulocytes (Moras et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Moras et al. 2017

claim: Reticulocytes develop into mature erythrocytes.
source: Early reticulocytes egress from the bone marrow and constitute 1–3% of circulating RBCs before they develop into mature erythrocytes (Chin-Yee et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from Chin-Yee et al. 1991

claim: Plasmodium parasites invade red blood cells for their asexual propagation.
source: In the mammalian host, plasmodia invade red blood cells (RBCs) for their asexual propagation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Plasmodium life cycle

claim: Plasmodium parasites favor different RBC maturation stages for their intraerythrocytic development depending on the species.
source: Depending on the species, the parasites favor different RBC maturation stages for their intraerythrocytic development.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Plasmodium biology
